examShortTricks: Trick 1: Monohybrid cross scaffold: TT × tt → all Tt (F1) → F2 3:1 (phenotype), 1:2:1 (genotype) — draw the Punnett square; the ratios ARE the marks.
Trick 2: Dihybrid: TtYy × TtYy → 9:3:3:1 — quote the law of independent assortment for the ratio; test cross with a double recessive gives 1:1:1:1.
Trick 3: Three laws in one line each: dominance (one allele masks), segregation (alleles separate in gametes), independent assortment (genes on different chromosomes assort freely).
Trick 4: Test cross identifies an unknown genotype: with a homozygous recessive, all-dominant offspring → parent homozygous; 1:1 → heterozygous.
keyPoints: Mendel's monohybrid cross gives a 3:1 phenotypic ratio in F2.
Dihybrid cross gives 9:3:3:1, proving independent assortment.
Alleles segregate during gamete formation.
A test cross with the recessive parent reveals the unknown genotype.
practiceQuestions: Q. In a cross between tall heterozygous pea plants, what fraction is dwarf? (2 marks) — Tt × Tt → 1/4 tt dwarf.
Q. State the law of independent assortment. (1 mark) — alleles of different genes assort independently during gamete formation.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Incomplete dominance: heterozygote is INTERMEDIATE (red × white snapdragon → pink); F2 = 1:2:1 both genotypic and phenotypic — the ratio change from 3:1 is the mark.
Trick 2: Codominance: BOTH alleles express fully (AB blood group: IA and IB codominant; i is recessive) — no blending, both products appear.
Trick 3: Blood group genotypes: A = IAIA or IAi; B = IBIB or IBi; AB = IAIB; O = ii — the table for the 2-mark question.
Trick 4: Distinguish in one phrase: incomplete = blended phenotype; codominance = both phenotypes side by side.
keyPoints: Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote shows a blended intermediate phenotype.
Codominance: both alleles are fully expressed together.
ABO blood groups illustrate codominance (IA/IB) and dominance (i recessive).
F2 ratios deviate from Mendel's 3:1 in both cases.
practiceQuestions: Q. Cross red (RR) and white (rr) snapdragons; give F1 and F2 phenotypes. (3 marks) — F1 all pink (Rr); F2 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
Q. Can a child of group O have parents AB and AB? (1 mark) — no; AB × AB gives only A, B or AB.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Linkage: genes on the SAME chromosome tend to inherit together, violating independent assortment; coupling phase (AB/ab) vs repulsion (Ab/aB).
Trick 2: Crossing over in pachytene of prophase-I produces recombinants; recombination frequency ∝ distance between genes (1 map unit = 1% recombination).
Trick 3: Strongly linked genes (close together) show FEWER recombinants; a test cross ratio near 1:1:1:1 means unlinked genes — read the data this way.
Trick 4: Significance: crossing over creates variation for evolution; linkage preserves favourable gene combinations.
keyPoints: Linked genes lie on the same chromosome and inherit together.
Crossing over during meiosis-I separates linked genes, producing recombinants.
Recombination frequency measures genetic distance.
Tightly linked genes show low recombination.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why did Mendel not observe linkage? (1 mark) — the seven traits he chose were on different chromosomes (or far apart).
Q. Two genes show 12% recombination — what does it mean? (1 mark) — they are 12 map units apart on the same chromosome.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Human sex determination: XX female, XY male; the father's sperm (X or Y) decides the sex — 50:50; state 'male is heterogametic'.
Trick 2: Haemophilia pedigree: affected father X^hY passes to ALL daughters (carriers) and NO sons; carrier mother × normal father → 50% sons affected — the two standard crosses.
Trick 3: Colour blindness is X-linked recessive; females need BOTH X's affected — hence males (hemizygous) suffer far more.
Trick 4: Other disorders for the list: sickle-cell anaemia (autosomal recessive, HbS), Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner (XO), Klinefelter (XXY).
keyPoints: Humans: XX = female, XY = male; sex is determined by the sperm.
Haemophilia and colour blindness are X-linked recessive disorders.
X-linked recessive disorders affect males more often.
Chromosomal disorders include Down (21 trisomy), Turner (XO) and Klinefelter (XXY).
practiceQuestions: Q. Why are haemophiliac males more common than females? (2 marks) — males have one X; a single recessive allele expresses, females need two.
Q. What is the sex of a child with XXY constitution? (1 mark) — male with Klinefelter syndrome.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Sutton and Boveri united Mendel with meiosis: genes are on chromosomes; segregation parallels homologue separation in anaphase-I; independent assortment parallels random metaphase alignment.
Trick 2: Two parallels to quote: (1) alleles pair → homologous chromosome pair; (2) allele separation → anaphase-I disjunction.
Trick 3: Evidence beyond it: chromosome mapping and sex linkage confirmed genes occupy specific chromosome loci.
keyPoints: Chromosome theory: genes are located on chromosomes.
Behaviour of chromosomes in meiosis explains Mendel's laws.
Sutton and Boveri proposed the theory (1902–03).
Homologous chromosome segregation mirrors allele segregation.
practiceQuestions: Q. State the chromosome theory of inheritance. (2 marks) — genes are carried on chromosomes whose meiotic behaviour explains Mendelian segregation.
Q. Which meiotic stage shows allele segregation physically? (1 mark) — anaphase-I (homologues separate).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: DNA structure in numbers: double helix, antiparallel, 2 nm wide, 3.4 nm per turn, 10 bp/turn; A=T, G≡C (Chargaff) — the numbers are the marks.
Trick 2: Replication: semi-conservative (Meselson–Stahl), 5'→3' synthesis, leading continuous/lagging Okazaki fragments, DNA polymerase + helicase + ligase — one line each.
Trick 3: Central dogma: DNA →(transcription, RNA polymerase)→ mRNA →(translation, ribosome + tRNA)→ protein; genetic code: triplet, degenerate, universal, non-overlapping.
Trick 4: tRNA cloverleaf carries the anticodon; Wobble pairs; start codon AUG, stops UAA/UAG/UGA — the code table essentials.
keyPoints: Watson–Crick double helix: antiparallel strands with complementary base pairing.
Replication is semi-conservative and bidirectional.
Transcription makes mRNA from a DNA template; translation decodes triplets into protein.
The genetic code is triplet, degenerate and universal.
practiceQuestions: Q. What proved DNA replication is semi-conservative? (1 mark) — Meselson–Stahl experiment with 15N/14CsCl gradients.
Q. If a DNA strand reads 3'-ATGC-5', the mRNA is? (2 marks) — 5'-UACG-3' (complementary, T→U).
Q. State two features of the genetic code. (1 mark) — triplet and degenerate (also universal).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: HGP facts: 1990–2003, 3.2 billion base pairs, ~20,000–25,000 genes, international consortium (US, UK, Japan, France, Germany, China) — the numbers are the marks.
Trick 2: Two approaches: expressed sequence tags (EST) and sequence annotation; methods: Sanger sequencing + BAC/YAC clones + overlaps.
Trick 3: Findings to quote: only ~2% codes for proteins; genes are unevenly distributed; SNP mapping; ~1.4 million SNPs identified.
Trick 4: Significance: medicine (gene therapy, pharmacogenomics), forensics, evolutionary comparison — three applications.
keyPoints: HGP sequenced the entire human genome (3.2 × 10⁹ bp).
Humans have about 20,000–25,000 protein-coding genes.
Less than 2% of the genome codes for proteins.
Outcomes: disease gene discovery, personalised medicine, forensic DNA profiling.
practiceQuestions: Q. How many base pairs does the human genome contain? (1 mark) — about 3.2 billion.
Q. Give two significances of the HGP. (1 mark) — locating disease genes; comparing human evolution with other species.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Evidences list: palaeontology (fossils), comparative anatomy (homologous/analogous organs), embryology (Haeckel), molecular (cytochrome c), biogeography — five with one line each.
Trick 2: Hardy–Weinberg: p² + 2pq + q² = 1 — p² = AA, 2pq = Aa, q² = aa; disturbed by mutation, migration, drift, selection, non-random mating — the five forces.
Trick 3: Adaptive radiation: Darwin's finches (beaks), Australian marsupials — one ancestor → many niches; convergent evolution is the analogous-organ flip side.
Trick 4: Human evolution order: Australopithecus → Homo habilis → H. erectus → Neanderthal → H. sapiens — brain size increases, jaw decreases.
keyPoints: Evolution evidences: fossils, homology, analogy, embryology, molecular homology.
Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium: p² + 2pq + q² = 1 in an ideal population.
Adaptive radiation produces many species from one ancestor (Darwin's finches).
Human evolution progressed from Australopithecus to Homo sapiens.
practiceQuestions: Q. In a population p = 0.7 — find the frequency of heterozygotes. (2 marks) — 2pq = 2×0.7×0.3 = 0.42.
Q. Distinguish homologous and analogous organs with examples. (2 marks) — forelimbs of man/whale (same origin) vs wings of bird/butterfly (same function).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Vector table — malaria: Plasmodium via female Anopheles; dengue: dengue virus via female Aedes; filariasis: Wuchereria via Culex; typhoid: Salmonella typhi (contaminated food/water); ascariasis: Ascaris (fecal-oral); pneumonia: Streptococcus/Diplococcus.
Trick 2: Symptoms one-liners: malaria — recurring chill and fever (every 48 h for P. vivax); typhoid — step-ladder fever, Widal test; filariasis — elephantiasis (lymph swelling).
Trick 3: Control pairs: mosquito-borne → nets, repellents, larvivorous fish; water-borne → safe drinking water, ORS, sanitation; the control answer mirrors the transmission route.
Trick 4: AIDS: HIV via sexual contact, infected needles, transfusion — NOT by touch; the 'not spread by' clause earns the mark.
keyPoints: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium and spread by female Anopheles.
Dengue spreads through Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.
Typhoid and pneumonia are bacterial; ascariasis is a helminth infection.
Prevention targets the vector or transmission route.
practiceQuestions: Q. Name the vector and causative organism of filariasis. (1 mark) — Wuchereria bancrofti via Culex mosquito.
Q. How is typhoid confirmed in the lab? (1 mark) — Widal test.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Innate (inborn, non-specific, 4 barriers: physical skin/mucus, physiological acid/tears, cellular WBC, cytokine) vs adaptive (acquired, specific, memory) — the two-column contrast is the whole answer.
Trick 2: Cell-mediated (T cells, graft rejection) vs humoral (B cells → antibodies) — name the two arms of adaptive immunity.
Trick 3: Active immunity (own antibodies, slow, long-lasting, vaccination) vs passive (borrowed antibodies, immediate, short, e.g. maternal IgG) — the comparison table.
Trick 4: AIDS attacks helper T cells → both arms fail — the immunology link line.
keyPoints: Innate immunity is inborn and non-specific; adaptive is acquired and specific.
Adaptive immunity has humoral (B-cell/antibody) and cell-mediated (T-cell) arms.
Active immunity develops after exposure; passive is transferred ready-made antibody.
Memory cells give long-lasting adaptive protection.
practiceQuestions: Q. Differentiate innate and adaptive immunity (two points). (2 marks) — non-specific/inborn vs specific/learned with memory.
Q. Which immunity rejects an organ transplant? (1 mark) — cell-mediated (T-cell) immunity.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Antigen = foreign molecule binding antibody/MHC; antibody = Y-shaped Ig (2 heavy + 2 light chains, disulphide bonds) with variable antigen-binding sites — draw the Y.
Trick 2: Ig classes: IgG (most abundant, crosses placenta), IgA (secretions), IgM (first response, pentamer), IgE (allergy), IgD — the five classes with one role each.
Trick 3: Primary vs secondary response: secondary is faster, stronger (memory cells) — the graph sketch earns marks.
Trick 4: Antibody actions: neutralisation, opsonisation, agglutination, complement lysis — four verbs, four marks.
keyPoints: Antigens trigger immune responses; antibodies neutralise them.
Antibody: Y-shaped glycoprotein with two heavy and two light chains.
Five immunoglobulin classes: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD.
Memory cells make the secondary response rapid and intense.
practiceQuestions: Q. Which antibody crosses the placenta? (1 mark) — IgG.
Q. Why is the secondary immune response faster? (1 mark) — memory B cells already exist.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Principle: harmless antigen → primary response → memory cells → rapid secondary response on real infection — the memory mechanism IS the answer.
Trick 2: Vaccine types: killed/inactivated (polio Salk), live attenuated (BCG, oral polio Sabin), toxoid (tetanus), subunit/recombinant (Hepatitis B) — one example each.
Trick 3: Passive immunisation: antivenom, immunoglobulin shots — immediate protection without memory.
Trick 4: National programmes: Pulse Polio, BCG at birth, DPT schedule — quote one for the applied mark.
keyPoints: Vaccination generates active immunity and immunological memory.
Vaccines may be killed, live-attenuated, toxoid or recombinant.
Passive immunisation gives ready-made antibodies (antivenom).
Immunisation programmes protect whole populations.
practiceQuestions: Q. How does a vaccine protect against future infection? (2 marks) — it induces memory B/T cells that respond rapidly to the real pathogen.
Q. Give one example of a live attenuated vaccine. (1 mark) — BCG (or oral polio Sabin).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Allergy = exaggerated IgE response to harmless antigens (pollen, dust); chemicals histamine and serotonin cause sneezing, watery eyes, rashes — name the chemicals.
Trick 2: Treatment: antihistamines (cetrizine), adrenaline for anaphylaxis — the two drugs to quote.
Trick 3: Autoimmunity: immune system attacks SELF (memory loss of self-tolerance) — rheumatoid arthritis, type-1 diabetes, lupus; quote two.
Trick 4: Hereditary angle: allergies run in families (atopy) — the genetic susceptibility line.
keyPoints: Allergy: hypersensitivity to normally harmless antigens via IgE and histamine.
Antihistamines relieve symptoms; adrenaline treats severe anaphylaxis.
Autoimmune diseases arise from loss of self-tolerance.
Examples: rheumatoid arthritis, insulin-dependent diabetes, lupus.
practiceQuestions: Q. Name the chemicals responsible for allergic symptoms. (1 mark) — histamine and serotonin.
Q. What is an autoimmune disease? (1 mark) — a condition in which the immune system attacks the body's own cells.
